# Facet checks from the card library

*Generated by `../library/build_index.py`. Each line is a card writer's note where the full text of a source says something other than a facet file says about it. Card writers wrote these before the S2 verification pass; where a card was later corrected, the card is the authority.*

234 notes across 234 cards.

## Facet A — The record

- [`tunbridge1992study`](../library/tunbridge1992study.md): the facet (A6) read only the abstract and called the thesis "independent of Saenger" and hedged ("may have"). The full text confirms a different method (grammar teaching and manuscript counts). It is stronger than the abstract on motive: "must be seen as a practical outcome" of the grammarians' study (p. 98) and "primarily a linguistic phenomenon" (Long Abstract p. 7). It is not independent of Parkes, who supervised it (Acknowledgements), and its dating of the earliest manuscripts rests on Brown and Lowe (p. 194, n. 3), so it adds no independent test of Saenger's chronology (premise P2).
## Facet B — The dispute

- [`garrett1998saenger`](../library/garrett1998saenger.md): the facet B entry matches my reading (strong-form restatement; page 487 for the co-constituent passage; page 488 for the continuum and screens sentences). No contradiction.
- [`heilmann2020reading`](../library/heilmann2020reading.md): facet B's reading of this chapter is accurate on every page I checked (pp. 178, 179, 180, 181, 182, 183, 190). One addition: Heilmann relies on Vatri for the Thai result and does not cite the 2009 study's sentence-level slowing, which Chantavarin and Leung (2025, `chantavarin2025effects`) report.
- [`ker2012johnson`](../library/ker2012johnson.md): facet B records this review as read in full and about 940 words; confirmed, with no pagination. Ker does not discuss training of novices, so the review gives K no purchase on Johnson's "emerging readers" sentence.
- [`knox1968silent`](../library/knox1968silent.md): facet B's report of the quotations and page numbers (pp. 421, 422, 427, 434–435) matches the text; the last printed page is 435, as the facet says. The facet's note that Knox "never mentions word separation" is confirmed.
- [`mannering2012johnson`](../library/mannering2012johnson.md): facet B says Mannering was read in part (opening, chapters 1–3, conclusion; chapters 4–9 skimmed). This card rests on the full review, and the full text confirms the facet's reading of chapters 1 and 2. The review never mentions Saenger, spacing as a medieval change, or Knox.
- [`odonnell1994parkes`](../library/odonnell1994parkes.md): facet B says the review "also records Saenger's 1982 *Viator* article as the pre-1997 form of the thesis." The 1994 review does not cite the *Viator* article. That reference is in O'Donnell's 2000 review of Saenger (`odonnell2000saenger`, second paragraph). The facet appears to have merged the two reviews. The rest of the facet's account (the missing-Saenger quotation and the read-aloud contrast) is accurate. The facet also calls the read "final paragraph(s)"; the whole review is short and has now been read.
- [`odonnell2000saenger`](../library/odonnell2000saenger.md): facet B's quotations of ¶2 and ¶3 match the text, including that "commonplace" in ¶2 is O'Donnell's own claim. The facet's description of the whole as four paragraphs is right.
- [`reis2011johnson`](../library/reis2011johnson.md): facet B lists it as read in full at about 300 words, which is right. The facet's description is neutral; the card flags that Reis's "ensured" is stronger than Ker's "consistent with."
## Facet C — Spacing to literacy

- [`becker2024conquering`](../library/becker2024conquering.md): the facet's quotation "Protestantism played a crucial role in the accumulation of human capital" does not appear in the open PDF I read (abstract or text); the printed abstract says Protestant church density predicts 1930 literacy and that Presbyterians did better than Methodists. The facet probably quoted an earlier or database abstract. Quote the printed abstract instead. A second flag: Becker and Won put the start of government efforts to teach Hangul at "the Gabo Reform in 1886" (p. 6), while Ivanova (`ivanova2026process`, p. 138) dates the Kabo reforms to 1894 and the first joint hangul-and-hanja newspaper to 1886. One of them has the date wrong or they mean different things.
- [`clemens2025korea`](../library/clemens2025korea.md): facet C says the figures are "the review's statements about the book." My reading is weaker: the figures are the reviewer's own, unsourced, and not marked as the book's. Do not describe them as what Cha and Pacheco Pardo report.
- [`ivanova2026process`](../library/ivanova2026process.md): facets C and F cite only the abstract, so the statements about spacing in the body are new to the project. The facet's "marginalized" quote is accurate.
- [`seymour2003foundation`](../library/seymour2003foundation.md): the facet quotes the abstract's "more than twice as slow." The body gives a ratio of about 2.5:1 and also two further points the facet does not record: letter-sound knowledge does not differ between languages, and the gap sits in word and nonword reading.
- [`ziegler2010orthographic`](../library/ziegler2010orthographic.md): the facet says the paper has "the same bearing as Seymour." It does not. It reports predictors of reading in Grade 2, not acquisition rates, and the study itself restricts its claim to alphabetic scripts and flags Chinese as unexplored (p. 557).
## Facet D — Reading science

- [`bai2008reading`](../library/bai2008reading.md): facet D marks this source "read in part." The full text adds no contradiction. It does add two things the facet might want: the null result is on N = 16 and N = 24 skilled adults only, and the "words are the unit" claim rests on character-spacing and nonword-spacing costs. The source says nothing about learners, so it cannot carry the learner half of P4.
- [`bassetti2012effects`](../library/bassetti2012effects.md): facet D marked this "read in part" and lists "no gain for children" correctly. The full text adds that the child effect is negative, not null, and that the adult hanzi slowdown depends on block order. The submitted version says of Bai et al. 2008 that they "found faster reading with interword spacing", which "probably happened because hanzi-spaced sentences occupied twice the width on screen compared with word-spaced sentences". That holds only against character spacing: in Bai's Table 1, word-spaced text took 5,239 ms and character-spaced text 5,686 ms, while normal unspaced text took 5,221 ms, so Bai found no gain over unspaced text. The width explanation is Bassetti and Masterson's, not a finding of Bai et al.
- [`chantavarin2025effects`](../library/chantavarin2025effects.md): the facet D entry gives only the reference, so there is no claim to contradict. It writes "et al."; the PDF confirms two authors, and `references.bib` already lists both. My reading qualifies `ARGUMENT_MAP.md` P4, as noted above.
- [`chen2021tradeoff`](../library/chen2021tradeoff.md): facet D (row "Practice") reads the abstract correctly, and I confirm the Experiment 2 null on total time and speed. The facet notes a corrigendum; the open copy I read carries none, so I cannot confirm that point.
- [`cui2023eye`](../library/cui2023eye.md): facet D's learner row (Cui 2023 listed as support, "Helps") overstates the result. The significant contrasts are against non-word and pinyin versions; the unspaced-against-word-spaced contrast is not significant.
- [`degno2019coregistration`](../library/degno2019coregistration.md): no contradiction. One reminder from the full text: "unspaced" means unspaced in the parafoveal preview, so the study does not show how an entire unspaced page reads.
- [`frey2026correlational`](../library/frey2026correlational.md): facet D uses Frey 2026 as the open source for 14–15 characters right and 3–4 left. That is an accurate quotation. The facet does not mention that the article's own measured perceptual span was 8.87 letters, well below the classical figure. The authors attribute the gap to wider letters (0.54° against 0.46° in earlier work) and suggest the span is more stable in degrees than in letters (PDF p. 8). Anyone quoting "14–15 characters" from Frey should know the same paper finds less in its own sample.
- [`galliussi2020inter`](../library/galliussi2020inter.md): the facet's one-line summary, "reading speed is impaired by an increase in inter-letter spacing not combined with an adequate increase in inter-word spacing," matches the abstract. It omits that the authors call the effect practically negligible (under 0.20 syll/s) and found no letterform effect.
- [`hakvoort2017improvements`](../library/hakvoort2017improvements.md): the facet quotes the abstract's "interword level" line. The body says "sentence level"; cite the body.
- [`hervais2019learning`](../library/hervais2019learning.md): the facet's quotations from the abstract and from the Results ("There is no obvious decrease in the magnitude of the peak response to any category of stimulus as a function of literacy") are exact. The facet's entry lists seven authors and omits Frank Eisner; the PDF and the bib record list eight.
- [`houpt2014new`](../library/houpt2014new.md): the facet's "read in part" status is consistent with what the paper contains. The one use is the Cattell sentence; the experiments are about single four-letter words in isolation, so the paper must not be cited for word-level processing in running text. It does support one narrow point for D6: word-level units are processed more efficiently than letter-by-letter, and the authors tie this to perceptual learning, not to any property of spacing.
- [`jordan2024reicher`](../library/jordan2024reicher.md): the facet cites seven authors with initials "Akkaya, S., Göçmüş, S., Kalan, Ö., Morgul, M. E., Önalan, M., & Sheen, M." The PDF and the bib record give Akkaya A. M., Göçmüş F. Z., Kalan A., Morgul E., Önalan K., Sheen M. K. The facet's quotations match the text.
- [`kohsom1997adding`](../library/kohsom1997adding.md): I find nothing in the paper that matches "gain nothing". The paper's own claim is a small gain for natives of an unspaced script and a large one for the second-language text. The large effect belongs to the English text, where readers have no practice without spaces, which fits P3 and the learners clause of P4.
- [`kubota2024rethinking`](../library/kubota2024rethinking.md): the facet's two quotations ("do not provide support" and recycling of cortex that processed "limbs") match the Abstract. The facet line is accurate and the full reading adds three cautions the facet omits: the sample of 10 in the before-and-after study, the finding that body-selective cortex stayed stable while limb-selective cortex was recycled, and the admission that evidence for lateralization of faces in preschoolers is inconsistent.
- [`kutas2011thirty`](../library/kutas2011thirty.md): facet D's quotations are exact and its "read in part" status is superseded. One quotation ("The N400 was labeled as such...") sits in Names and definitions, not the introduction.
- [`mirault2019precise`](../library/mirault2019precise.md): the facet lists this paper as "not read", relying on a secondary summary that transpositions hurt unspaced reading more. The full text confirms that summary, and adds that the interaction was absent in first-fixation and gaze duration and was weaker when boundary letters were frequent.
- [`mirault2019reading`](../library/mirault2019reading.md): the facet lists this paper as abstract only (HAL blocked); the full text confirms the abstract quotations. The facet's open item on the "40–70%" range is resolved: the range appears on p. 22, and the authors attribute it to Rayner & Pollatsek (1996) and Rayner et al. (1998), not to their own data.
- [`ozkan2026wordinitial`](../library/ozkan2026wordinitial.md): the facet's abstract-level reading ("initial capitals restored lexical processing but not all of the oculomotor cost") overstates one thing. The design has no lowercase spaced baseline and no unspaced lowercase condition, so it cannot show what capitals restore relative to ordinary text; it shows only that the frequency effect is the same size with and without spaces once capitals are present. The authors say as much: the design "does not test any additional cost or benefit that word-initial capitals themselves may impose relative to ordinary lowercase spaced text" (Discussion, PDF p. 11). The global reading-time cost also remained (about 7%, by my arithmetic from Table 2).
- [`perea2012subtle`](../library/perea2012subtle.md): the facet's one-line summary, "Fixations briefest at +1.5 spacing in skilled readers," is correct and omits that total reading time did not follow.
- [`price2011interactive`](../library/price2011interactive.md): the facet quotes the Abstract line on orthography emerging "from regional interactions", and the quotation is exact. The facet records the paper as read in part (abstract and opening); the full reading adds that the account is a framework argued from existing studies, not a new experiment, and that it explicitly sets itself against Dehaene's recycling and bigram-detector proposals. It also makes the point that task and attention reverse selectivity, which weakens any claim that vOT activation shows "word-specific" tuning.
- [`wagemans2012century`](../library/wagemans2012century.md): the facet's quotation matches §3.1 and its "read in part" status is superseded. Its summary that word spaces "work by proximity grouping, the oldest grouping principle" is the facet agent's inference, not this review's.
- [`wang2024tibetan`](../library/wang2024tibetan.md): the facet lists this paper in D without a note on its findings. The reading confirms spacing helps; it does not support "no gain for fluent readers".
- [`wertli2023influence`](../library/wertli2023influence.md): the facet row calling the "7 – 9 characters" statement secondhand is correct. The perceptual-span figures in the Introduction are likewise taken from other work.
- [`winskel2009eye`](../library/winskel2009eye.md): the facet cites the paper for the cost of removing spaces. That is correct. The facet does not mention the Thai result, which is the more informative one for the unspaced-script debate: a 5% slowdown at sentence level with a word-level gain, and large differences between readers.
- [`yu2023altered`](../library/yu2023altered.md): the facet describes the paper as one of three open papers that restate the perceptual-span figures. That is accurate. Yu and Kwon contribute a different number too: the span they measure in this task is about 11 to 14 letters, which they call "slightly" smaller than the perceptual span of 14 to 19 letters, and they give reasons (Discussion).
## Facet E — Human-factors frame

- [`clark1998extended`](../library/clark1998extended.md): the abstract does not cite this paper; facet E lists it only as a pointer. Nothing in the text concerns reading, writing or conventions.
- [`dewinter2014fitts`](../library/dewinter2014fitts.md): facet X called the pair "record verified; not read." Its gloss of the critique, that moving work "changes the work and the person's role," is borne out at §3.2.1 and §4, but the authors reject the critique's conclusion for the Fitts list. Facet E rightly notes that function allocation presumes two agents; a page is not an agent, and this paper does not extend the frame to representations.
- [`erickson2000social`](../library/erickson2000social.md): the facet describes this card's content accurately (pp. 61–62, abstract, "I know that you know that I know you are there"). The facet read only pp. 59–62; the rest adds the constraint argument, the privacy tension (§2.2, "translucent" not "transparent"), and the Babble evidence, which the facet did not use. The facet's "one anecdote and a chat system" is right but undercounts: the paper has several vignettes (restaurant, reception, wine shop, book-ordering workshop, limerick game).
- [`hutchins1995cockpit`](../library/hutchins1995cockpit.md): the facet's bearing statement agrees with my reading. Its read status ("in part, pp. 265, 277, 280–283") is now superseded by a full reading, and nothing in the rest of the article contradicts the facet's quotations. The facet quotations I compared (pp. 277, 280, 282, 283) match the text.
- [`kirsh1995intelligent`](../library/kirsh1995intelligent.md): the facet reads Kirsh's agent as arranging its own workspace and the scribe as arranging another's, and treats this as a gap in fit. Kirsh's text is less sharp than that. He says arrangements cue "cognitive events or processes in himself or herself, or another agent", and his example is supermarket managers who bias "consumer choice" with displays; his fourth assumption says work environments are pre-structured by others for the agent. So an arrangement made by one party for another is inside Kirsh's frame. The supermarket case is also one in which the arranger's interest differs from the shopper's, which touches **P10** and ruling D8, though Kirsh does not draw that out. The facet's quotations match the web text exactly.
- [`kirshmaglio1994distinguishing`](../library/kirshmaglio1994distinguishing.md): facet E's reading (epistemic action is something the agent does to its own task) matches pp. 513-514. Facet I's three quotations are exact. Its page ranges are slightly wide (the chess passage is p. 545, not 543–546; "Experts keep their costs lower" is p. 547). Facet I says the player "already knows" the rules; the paper supports this through p. 543 but also notes that players do not know they use the column cue (p. 529). Facet I does not give the sample size behind the 800–1200 ms figure: three players, a pilot, "we estimate" (p. 530).
- [`larkin1987why`](../library/larkin1987why.md): facet F lists Larkin and Simon as "Not read"; this card supersedes that. Facet E's quotations and pages match the text. Facet E's wording "informationally equivalent, computationally unequal" is a fair gloss of p. 67, but the paper's own definition of computational equivalence includes the informational condition and is about "easily and quickly", which the authors call "not precise terms" (p. 67).
- [`pea1985beyond`](../library/pea1985beyond.md): facet E marked this "abstract only" and called it "an independent, earlier statement of the amplifier-versus-reorganizer contrast." The full text confirms that, and shows the contrast is built on Cole and Griffin (1980), which the facet did not know.
- [`risko2016cognitive`](../library/risko2016cognitive.md): the facet says the definition "requires the person's own physical action, so it does not cover a scribe's spacing." The definition does say physical action, but Box 3 includes built-in offloading, so the facet should say the review also covers designer-built cases. Its other quotations and the Box 3 cost list match the text. The facet cites the definition at ms. p. 2; it is also on p. 3.
- [`scaife1996external`](../library/scaife1996external.md): the facet's two definitions are exact. It cites the "presumed benefits" and "even less understanding" quotations to pp. 209–210; in the pagination I read both are on p. 210. The facet's reading of the practice point is supported by the full text and by pp. 195, 199 and 208.
- [`termuende2025impact`](../library/termuende2025impact.md): the facet read only the abstract, the introduction and the start of the background, and says the introduction "states Saenger's account as settled" and that the authors may not discuss his critics. Fuller reading: §9.1 hedges the same account and notes the opposing evidence, though the paper never names Saenger's critics (it cites Saenger once). Second, the facet quotes the abstract's range "between 32.7ms—color technique—and 70.7ms—connection technique". Those two figures appear only in the abstract; I found neither in the body, whose ranges are 25–84 ms (Exp. 1), about 17–63 ms (Exp. 3) and "at least 17ms" in the conclusion (§10). The facet's other points hold: the paper tests sub-word cues, not word spacing, and "192 participants" is a count of collected datasets (48 + 48 + 96) that includes Exp. 2, whose results are withheld.
- [`vicente1992ecological`](../library/vicente1992ecological.md): facets E and I read parts of IV.A, V.A and V.B and quote them accurately; I found nothing contradicting their lines. I did not compare the manuscript with the journal text.
- [`zhang1994representations`](../library/zhang1994representations.md): the facet and the argument map cite the definition of the representational effect at p. 89. In the journal pagination it sits at p. 88 (the heading "The Representational Effect" opens p. 88; p. 89 holds the list of problem-isomorph studies and the "Distributed Representations" principle). The p. 118 quotation is correct. The facet does not mention that the paper is silent on text, reading or writing; I found no passage on any of them.
## Facet F — Parallel moves

- [`biggs2020decoding`](../library/biggs2020decoding.md): facet F read the introduction line as a finding that the visible notation lagged the working one. The body does not establish it. In §4 Biggs says no firm answer exists on when the officers learned the methods (p. 9), and the multiplications he decodes are within reach of an abacus (p. 8). The lag is his premise, not something the records show. The facet also names the journal *British Journal for the History of Mathematics*; the manuscript says *BSHM Bulletin*, as the bib note records.
- [`buijsman2020numerals`](../library/buijsman2020numerals.md): facet F wrote "The cost saving of place value shows up with practice and with column layout." Buijsman's text contains neither point. The practice claim has no support here, and the column point comes from Menary's multiplication layouts (pp. 3786–3787) without a cost figure. The facet's quotation of Krajcsi and Szabó is accurate; the sentence runs from the foot of p. 3787 to the top of p. 3788.
- [`buncic2017factors`](../library/buncic2017factors.md): facet F quotes the abstract accurately, and the body makes the same two points (pp. 26, 39–41). Its counter-case row names "installed base" and "the revolutionary bundle" as Bunčić's causes of failure. The installed-base point is there (p. 36). The revolutionary bundle is not; Bunčić does not treat reforms as bundles, and the phrase belongs to the facet.
- [`dacosta2018tabulae`](../library/dacosta2018tabulae.md): facet F rests on the published abstract, which this manuscript lacks, so I could not match its phrase "marketed these features as time-saving innovations." The body does show printers selling tables as quick finding aids (p. 17). It adds what the abstract lacks: the 11% and 33-of-225 figures, and printers from 1485 to 1528 explaining reference schemes to readers at length (pp. 10–12).
- [`danna2022numerical`](../library/danna2022numerical.md): the facet quotes the abstract's "over 1050 manuals". The body gives two counts: over 1,290 in the full dataset (p. 9) and 1,054 in the 815-city growth sample (p. 13). The facet's quotation of p. 5 ("no direct evidence of the first adoption … surely had been adopted by the end of the 13th century") is exact. The facet is silent on the main limitation below.
- [`haines2008origins`](../library/haines2008origins.md): the facet's two quotations (p. 331 "untenable … self-promotion"; the "popularization" sentence) are exact; the second falls on p. 344. The facet records a partial read; the full text adds that Guido's own contribution is dated only through manuscripts from the late 11th or early 12th century, since no copy of the prologue survives from his time (p. 345), so any claim about what Guido proposed rests on later copies.
- [`hangeulmuseum`](../library/hangeulmuseum.md): the facet's 78% (1945) and 4.1% (1958) quotations are exact, and so is the surveys caveat. The page gives no source for the 78% or 4.1% figures, and the facet's own note that other sources give a different 1945 figure applies.
- [`margono1987study`](../library/margono1987study.md): the facet's figures (30 novices, 5.77 and 4.80 min at p < 0.10, errors p < 0.01, 18 against 10 preferring the Macintosh) match the text. The facet's caveat that the comparison confounds interface style with machine is correct and the source never addresses it: the Macintosh and PC differ in screen, keyboard and mouse as well (§1.3). The satisfaction figure rests on an ad hoc composite, and the time difference is significant only at p < 0.10. The test time is under five minutes in both conditions.
- [`nothaft2020satanic`](../library/nothaft2020satanic.md): the facet read only the 1299 and Padua section and the abstract. The full text confirms its account of Article 102 and of the pages. It adds that the Paduan rule dates from 1331, not 1348, and that Nothaft treats the motive for 1299 as unknown; Nothaft lists fraud-prevention as a "popular" explanation for 1299 but does not endorse it (p. 15, n. 22).
- [`park2025dokkyo`](../library/park2025dokkyo.md): the facet marks this a forum abstract; the page confirms it and shows it contains no counts or rates, so it cannot be cited for literacy levels.
- [`ryan2014historical`](../library/ryan2014historical.md): facet F, working from the abstract, took this note as part of the evidence that the big causal claim "was contested for decades by Yamey, and recent economic historians restrict double entry to control of debt and agents." Ryan does neither. He defends the causal claim at the macro level and says nothing about control of debt or agents. The abstract hides this by saying only that the note will "review Yamey's criticisms." Cite Ryan for the summary of Yamey and the two-centuries point, not for the deflation of Sombart. Sangster (2025; `sangster2025reboot`) supplies the criticism of Yamey's own definitions.
- [`sangster2024emergence`](../library/sangster2024emergence.md): The facet had only the abstract. Reading the whole text, I find the abstract-level claims intact, with five qualifications. (1) The facet says the 1211 ledger "has" double entries and so double entries are "nearly 280 years older" than Pacioli (1494 minus 1211 is 283). That holds only under Sangster's input definition; under the output definition earlier historians used, the earliest case is 1340 (p. 501). Contra entries almost never survive, and double entry is confirmed mainly from cross-references and offset (p. 506). (2) The facet says Sangster takes apart the "Pacioli" one-agent story. The text never discusses Pacioli's *Summa*; the name appears only in the title of a cited article (n. 48, Ciambotti 2016). Sangster targets the Yamey–Besta–Sombart definitional tradition, not Pacioli. The Pacioli comparison is the facet's, so the table row and the "Pacioli introduced double entry" item (F, lines 291 and 324) should not attribute it to Sangster. (3) He dates the origin to the twelfth century, earlier than 1211; the ledger is evidence of a method already running. (4) On "double entry produced capitalism," Sangster does not rebut it. He reports Yamey's view and cites Yamey 1949, p. 103, for the claim that credit dealings led to systematic accounting (n. 154, p. 523). (5) The facet gives the sentence "the reason for such a detailed bookkeeping method is unknown" in quotation marks; the abstract reads "The reason for the emergence of such a detailed bookkeeping method is unknown." No contradiction of substance.
- [`sangster2025reboot`](../library/sangster2025reboot.md): (1) Facet F attaches "a ledger of 1211 … and entity-wide double entry … by the end of the 13th century" to "Sangster 2025 [online 2024], abstract." Those details belong to `sangster2024emergence` (*Economic History Review*). Here 1211 is the earliest paragraph-format ledger (p. 378), and the confirmed double-entry dates are 1296 and 1299. (2) The facet lists Yamey's contest against Sombart as support for deflating the causal claim. Sangster does not overturn Yamey's finding that few identified profit before 1800; the abstract concurs. He argues that Yamey's definitions and synonyms invite readers to take it as a finding about bookkeeping (pp. 373–374). So Sangster qualifies how Yamey can be cited, and does not reject the Sombart criticism.
- [`schlimm2008modeling`](../library/schlimm2008modeling.md): I found no contradiction with the facet entry in `F_parallel_moves.md`. Its summary (four agents, 1,000,000 and 10,000 problems, no human data, "precise format of external inputs", the abacus caveat) matches pp. 2098–2102. The entry gives the p. 2097 quotation and the p. 2102 quotation correctly.
- [`shneiderman1983direct`](../library/shneiderman1983direct.md): the facet entry marks the article "read in part" and omits the "Problems with direct manipulation" section (p. 64) and the cited experiments; it is otherwise accurate. Its quotations (p. 57 definition; p. 59 on VisiCalc) match the page images. It says Roberts's figure and the office-automation evaluations were not checked; I did not check them either.
- [`strunk1998guido`](../library/strunk1998guido.md): no contradiction with `F_parallel_moves.md`. The facet's quotations match the workbook (pp. 2–5). One addition: the Prologue excerpt does describe the ruled lines, letters and colours (p. 3), so the staff itself is in the excerpt, though the facet's "Epistola ... not about the ruled staff" is correct for the *Epistola*. The workbook titles the second text "Epistolo"; the bib and facet give *Epistola*.
## Facet G — Nadella and his lineage

- [`alahmadi2022false`](../library/alahmadi2022false.md): facet G's summary matches the text (20 survey, 21 interviews, the 99% quote, benign triggers, Target, the abstract's "Alarm validation is a tedious task..."). The facet's own caution that 99% is "one analyst's figure" is correct: B3's statement; the survey's ten disclosed ratios were 1 real alert in 100 and 50 in 200 for two respondents, not a measured rate (p. 2788). I found no contradiction, but the facet's placement of the paper under "approval fatigue" evidence is looser than the text, which studies alarm validation, not approval.
- [`ancker2017effects`](../library/ancker2017effects.md): facet G summarises the study as showing alert fatigue "is therefore more about repeated and uninformative alerts than raw volume." That overstates two things. The number of BPAs per encounter was a strong predictor (IRR 0.70), so alert volume per encounter did matter; what showed no effect was overall workload, measured by patients and encounters. And "uninformative" is a proxy: the authors measured repetition, not informativeness, and say so (p. 3). The facet's quotations from the abstract are accurate.
- [`anderson1972computer`](../library/anderson1972computer.md): I find the facet's account accurate. Its quotations from §3.1, §3.2, §3.2.2 and §3.7 match the text and pages. The facet's "read in part" is now a full read of Volume I. One point to add: the facet cites section numbers that the table of contents gives differently from the body (see Caution).
- [`anthropic2026how`](../library/anthropic2026how.md): the bib note said "read in part (opening paragraphs)"; the full page was read here. Vendor report on its own product; the 52 real overeager actions come from employee denials and post-hoc flags, a small sample that depends on what was caught. The 93% is a rate of approvals, not a measure of inattention, and the post gives no behavioural measure of fatigue. The bib's note that "the drafting model is an Anthropic model" is not a statement the page makes.
- [`baker2025monitoring`](../library/baker2025monitoring.md): facet G lists Baker as "abstract only"; the full text confirms its summary line. The facet ties Korbak et al. to P9's "neuralese" worry; Baker raises the possibility that an agent "could learn a new language that is illegible to a monitor" (p. 8) without using the word.
- [`cert2022common`](../library/cert2022common.md): the facet's quotations from the definition, the 3,000-incident base, and Best Practice 12 are accurate. The facet says the practice 12 passages "cut against reading observe everything (P15) as literal full-volume human review"; that is right for the opening, but the same practice supports retrospective human review and full-time monitors (pp. 84, 89), so the guide supports the post's principle 15 (after-the-fact reconstruction) more than the facet suggests. The facet read only the titles of practices 5, 8 and 21; I read the text of 21 and only the opening pages of 5 and 8, and they confirm the facet's description (stress, negative environments, positive incentives to align the workforce) without changing it. I found no direct contradiction.
- [`chan2024visibility`](../library/chan2024visibility.md): the facet reading (identifier visible to the other party; human review left to "other work", citing Green) holds. The facet says Chan reaches counterparties where the post faces the enterprise only; in Chan the counterparty sees the identifier and agent card, not the monitoring or logs. The bib note says sections 4–5 and the appendix were unread; I read them.
- [`chan2025infrastructure`](../library/chan2025infrastructure.md): the facet cites this paper only for the definition (abstract-only read). The full text also carries the oversight-layer, moral-hazard and lock-in material above, which bears on P10 and P12 more than the facet shows.
- [`chen2025reasoning`](../library/chen2025reasoning.md): the facet (abstract only) gives "across six hint types ... at least 1% ... often below 20%"; the abstract says "for most settings and models tested". The body gives 5 of 6 settings for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 6 of 6 for R1 (p. 6). The facet's wording is slightly wider than the source.
- [`chen2026comparing`](../library/chen2026comparing.md): the facet (abstract only) matches the body on N, the 192 sessions and the quoted finding. It omits that the plan effect came partly from changing the agent.
- [`constantin2026nadella`](../library/constantin2026nadella.md): the bib note says the article date "is not shown in the fetched text". The saved page shows October 12, 2026, 7:55 am; update the bib entry. TNW's claims about Suleyman's earlier Bloomberg remark, Musk, Lieu, the "Super Intelligence Force" and the Anthropic incident are its own reporting and were not checked against their sources. The page is a journalist's paraphrase; do not quote it as Nadella's words except where it quotes the post.
- [`crootof2023humans`](../library/crootof2023humans.md): The facet's quotations and page numbers (pp. 472, 483, abstract) match the printed pagination. The facet's bearing on P19, "a human inserted to answer for the system," reads only one of the nine roles. A halt right is a resilience role in this typology, and the same person can hold both roles (p. 474).
- [`duzan2026chain`](../library/duzan2026chain.md): the facet's numbers (41–46 points in two of four settings; as low as 5%) match the body. The facet's phrase "monitoring helps, depends on conditions" is fair; but the paper's headline direction is that the conditions most like real deployment are the ones where it helps least.
- [`elish2019moral`](../library/elish2019moral.md): the facet (abstract and introduction only) states the definition correctly. Nothing contradicts it. The full text adds the TMI interface point and the certification argument, which the facet does not use.
- [`gema2026chain`](../library/gema2026chain.md): the facet's summary of the abstract (higher unverbalized adoption for tool returns; telling models they are monitored "does not reliably close the gap") holds. The body adds that the narrowing under the directive prompt is partly an increase in user-channel unverbalized adoption, so a smaller gap can mean worse behaviour on the other channel (pp. 13–14).
- [`green2022flaws`](../library/green2022flaws.md): the facet's reading (41 policies; people unable to perform oversight; remedy institutional, "not user engagement") holds. One qualification: Green says better oversight design is possible and an "open empirical question" (p. 11), so he does not say oversight can never work.
- [`greenblatt2024ai`](../library/greenblatt2024ai.md): the facet's reading is correct (human simulated by GPT-4; "up to 2%" is an evaluation parameter; the Table 2 numbers match). Facet G lists the read status as "in part"; the full body agrees with what the facet took from it.
- [`grundemclaughlin2026overseeing`](../library/grundemclaughlin2026overseeing.md): Facet G (abstract only) says the new interface "cut time to find errors". The body is weaker. The overall time effect is small and its interval spans zero. The larger effect (g = −0.65) applies to the subset where participants correctly judged a wrong answer wrong, and its interval (−1.54 to 0.12) also spans zero (Table 3, p. 18). Only the confidence effect on wrong-judged-right items has an interval clear of zero. The facet's accuracy and confidence statements stand.
- [`hao2024training`](../library/hao2024training.md): Facet G's summary (train models to reason in a continuous latent space) is accurate. The body adds that Coconut trails language chain of thought on GSM8k (34.1% against 42.9%), which an abstract-only reading would miss.
- [`jakkal2026secure`](../library/jakkal2026secure.md): the bib note says it was read via a WebFetch summary; the full page text was read here. The facet's "blocking after compromise signals is automated" is not stated: the page says security teams use the signals to "block agent actions" and does not say whether a person or the system blocks. A marketing page; no evidence of effect is offered, and "double agents" is its risk metaphor.
- [`jia2026faithfulness`](../library/jia2026faithfulness.md): Facet G read this as abstract only and describes the 2026 preprints as a group (monitoring "helps, depends on conditions, and degrades"). The full text agrees with that gloss for this paper, with one addition: the gains are in visibility of the shortcut, not in its prevention.
- [`kokotajlo2025ai`](../library/kokotajlo2025ai.md): facet G quotes the neuralese sentence correctly and calls the page "a forecast scenario, not a finding"; both hold. Facet G says the page "popularised the word". The page says only "We call this 'neuralese'" and credits Hao et al. (2024) for "implementing this idea"; it does not claim to coin or popularise the term, and I could not verify priority from it. Facet G also omits that the page says no frontier lab had adopted the technique.
- [`korbak2025chain`](../library/korbak2025chain.md): Facet G says the post's P9 "non-negotiable" matches Korbak's "recommend[s] ... investment in CoT monitoring". The paper is more guarded. It recommends investment "alongside existing safety methods" (abstract) and "only as an addition to existing safety research directions and not as a replacement" (§5, p. 7). The paper does not call monitoring non-negotiable. The facet's quotations from the abstract and the "fragile" theme are accurate.
- [`kroll2021outlining`](../library/kroll2021outlining.md): Facet G read only the abstract and introduction. The body supports its gloss that this is "the best formal statement" of what P15 asks. It adds that Kroll's records are mostly about design and development, with operations covered in §3.3, and that he treats the human-understanding requirement as unsolved.
- [`kumari2026nadella`](../library/kumari2026nadella.md): it attributes to Nadella that organisations decide "when human approval is required", and gives an example of a model that "may recommend a transaction, for example, without being allowed to approve or execute it independently". Neither phrase appears in the post; no approval step appears in P1–P21. They are the reporter's elaboration and should not be cited as Nadella's. On the debate, the article offers no critique of the post, only a note that agreement is not industry-wide.
- [`kutasov2025shade`](../library/kutasov2025shade.md): Facet G (abstract only) lists the paper under monitor models, and its synthesis says of the safety work it covers that it "does not test the human reader at all" (C3). For this paper that is wrong in a narrow way: Appendix L and §4.1 report a human baseline. The facet's abstract numbers (27%, 15%, AUC 0.87) are right.
- [`langer2024effective`](../library/langer2024effective.md): Facet G (abstract only) summarizes it as "a signal-detection framework for error detection by overseers". That is right, and it should be cited as a framework paper; there are no data in it.
- [`lanham2023measuring`](../library/lanham2023measuring.md): Facet G's quotation from the abstract is exact and its read status (abstract and introduction) understates what the body adds: the size result is per task, with 6 of 8 tasks peaking at 13B and AQuA and LogiQA the exceptions (p. 7), and the "less faithful" finding is for a multiple-choice setting with a fixed prompt format.
- [`laux2024institutionalised`](../library/laux2024institutionalised.md): Facet G quotes only the abstract sentence about unreliable overseers. The body qualifies it (the empirical record is "subject to debate"), and the paper is a proposal that offers no new empirical test.
- [`layman2023controlled`](../library/layman2023controlled.md): Facet G quotes the abstract exactly ("47% lower precision and 40% slower time on task"). The body shows the 47 is in percentage points of median precision, so a reader who takes it as a relative drop would understate the fall (about 59% in relative terms). Facet G does not mention that the sensitivity difference was not significant at p = .098 with 7 true alarms in the high-false-alarm group, so sensitivity is estimated on few items; this is my observation from the design, not a claim in the paper.
- [`little2026length`](../library/little2026length.md): facet G says monitoring "degrades under pressures the deployer can introduce by accident." In Little the pressure is a training objective, set by whoever fine-tunes the model, and the cost saving is deliberate; the monitorability loss is the side effect the token-accuracy criterion does not count (p. 1). It reaches a deployer only if the deployer trains. The full text bears out the abstract claims facet G recorded. The 39% and 35% figures are relative falls on MMLU-Pro-R at the 30% target, and the paper's own primary contrast is the 50% target (p. 5), which shows smaller falls (for Qwen3-14B the faithfulness score falls by 9 to 15 points, p. 2).
- [`lynch2025agentic`](../library/lynch2025agentic.md): facet G says that in Lynch "the model has its own goals," while the post's model has "mistakes or compromise." The paper complicates this: a threat to continued operation alone was enough, with no goal given (p. 8), and the authors say they cannot tell how far self-preservation, faulty reasoning or suspicion of the setup drove it (p. 9). They also say role-play may explain part of it (fn. 4, p. 3). Facet G's "abstract only" is now replaced by a full reading of the body.
- [`mitchell2026agents`](../library/mitchell2026agents.md): facet Z quotes the abstract ("impede effective human oversight," "design-level affordances") and notes that none of the oversight-fallacy sources "replaces the human check with structure." That holds for the headline, but the inventory includes structural items (bounded autonomy, automated pre-checks, separated roles), so Mitchell sits closer to the structural camp than facet Z's summary suggests. Facet G calls it a paper "arguing that agent design degrades the overseer's skills"; it argues that design both obstructs oversight (Section 3) and erodes it (Section 4).
- [`parasuraman2010complacency`](../library/parasuraman2010complacency.md): facet G says the studies are "lab and simulator work with one operator and one automation." Mostly, but the review also draws on accident reports (Royal Majesty, pp. 382-383), field trials of physicians (p. 394) and two team studies (p. 397). Facet G also says the brake-holder in P19 "is the person these studies describe." The review is narrower. Complacency is "typically found under conditions of multiple-task load" (p. 387; also the Abstract, p. 381). When participants only backed up the automation, detection was "near perfect" (p. 384), and in the single-failure study most single-task participants detected it (p. 385). The brake-holder who has no competing task is the weaker case for complacency. Against that, the authors expect worse monitoring at the very low failure rates of real systems, citing an estimate of one critical signal every two weeks (p. 385), so a dedicated watcher does not escape the problem. Automation bias, which needs no multitask load, is closer to the P15 reader.
- [`rieder2020towards`](../library/rieder2020towards.md): facet G says Rieder and Hofmann "agree with Nadella that the black box will not be opened; both choose observation of behaviour." Half right. They agree the box will not simply open, and they favour observing behaviour over time (pp. 13-14). But they do not choose observation in place of transparency; they say it is not "a radical departure" from it (p. 21) and that traditional disclosure, reports and whistleblowing can remain "part of an observability framework" (p. 13). The facet read the article in part; the full text adds the access-control argument above, which the facet did not record.
- [`rose2020zero`](../library/rose2020zero.md): facet G's quotations of tenets 3, 6 and 7 and its description of the decision and enforcement points hold against the full text. Its note that tenet 7 feeds "policy, not a human reader" also holds, with two additions from sections it did not read: administrator audit of the policy components (p. 28), and §7.3.7's line that "the subjects and stakeholders of the resources and processes involved should also provide feedback" (p. 41), which places enterprise users in a feedback role.
- [`saltzer1975protection`](../library/saltzer1975protection.md): every S&S quotation in facets G and X matches the text (least privilege, complete mediation, separation of privilege, psychological acceptability, open design, compromise recording, "warnings"). Facet G's status line "read in part (section I.A)" understates what I now confirm: the facets did not use the hierarchical-control passage, I.B.4 on authentication, or III.B.
- [`santonidesio2018meaningful`](../library/santonidesio2018meaningful.md): facet G says the abstract names "the humans designing and deploying" and that it did not read whether the body adds the affected. The body adds them only partly. The tracked agents are left open ("the relevant human agents", p. 11), with the only worked example the traffic case, where the system should follow rules set "by the society via the public authority" and unwritten conventions that "reflect some relevant interest of the road users" (pp. 11-12). So the road users' interest is in view, through public rules, not as a direct party to control. Tracing's condition (b) brings others in as people who may react morally to the responsible human (p. 9).
- [`sterz2024quest`](../library/sterz2024quest.md): facet G says P19 supplies (a) and P15 is meant to supply (b), and that the literature is about whether (b) and (c) hold. That matches the paper. The facet does not mention (d), fitting intentions, or role conflict (p. 8), which bear most directly on D5.
- [`stohl2016managing`](../library/stohl2016managing.md): The facet's attributes, paradox definition and p. 133 quotation are correct. It names only the inadvertent path; the strategic path (pp. 133–34) is the one closer to Nadella's seat. It marks the card "read in part"; I read the whole article.
- [`turan2026oversight`](../library/turan2026oversight.md): facet G calls it "a model of a fatiguing reviewer." True, and the paper also reports a measured disagreement result (κ = 0.52), though from LLM personas, not people (pp. 5, 9). Facet G's other statement, that the paper calls the results modelling results, holds in the body (pp. 1, 6, 9).
- [`turpin2023language`](../library/turpin2023language.md): the facet's "drop[s] by as much as 36%" is correct but is a drop of 36.3 accuracy points in one setting (GPT-3.5, zero-shot, Suggested Answer), not a relative loss. Claude 1.0's matching figure is 30.6 points, and the Answer-is-Always-A drops are far smaller (18.7 and 4.7 points; p. 6).
- [`wang2026monitorbench`](../library/wang2026monitorbench.md): the facet lists MonitorBench among "2026 preprints" read as abstracts. The full text carries a COLM 2026 header (v4), so "preprint, not peer reviewed" understates its status. I did not verify the acceptance beyond that header.
- [`yu2026habituation`](../library/yu2026habituation.md): the facet's numbers (400 reviewers, 11,429 reviews, 30.1% to 36.8%, latency 3.5 times, comments −22%) match the full text. The paper itself is less internally tidy than its abstract: the early-late change-request rates (11.2% to 5.6%) repeat the first-decile and tenth-decile figures of Table 1, the text says "28% less commenting" for words but 22% for comments (pp. 3–4), and Spearman ρ = +0.02 for PR size is given a p of 0.009 and called negligible (p. 4). I could not resolve these from the text.
## Facet H — Candidate moves

- [`alavi2026when`](../library/alavi2026when.md): the facet's quotations are accurate. The facet's closing line, "Counter-delegation creates a privacy channel", does not appear in the text: I searched for "counter-delegation" and found nothing. The defences are named as the three above (p. 18). The facet's "lets a seller infer" also compresses the design: a separate inference agent, not the seller, produces the estimates.
- [`alfrink2023contestable`](../library/alfrink2023contestable.md): the facet says "abstract only... No measured effects." The full text confirms there are no measured effects and adds the screening counts above. The facet's note that Crossref dates the paper 2022 while the key says 2023 is right: online 2022, volume year 2023.
- [`allouah2026what`](../library/allouah2026what.md): The facet's list of findings matches the text. Two omissions matter for citing it. First, the seller gain is not general: it occurs in 33% of category-model pairs and sometimes reverses (p. 22). Second, the authors report that basic rationality has become near-perfect (p. 13); the instability is in preferences and position, not in competence. The facet's line that these are "properties the person can no longer see" is the project's inference, since no person appears in the study. The headless replication used three August-generation models only.
- [`amin2026conversations`](../library/amin2026conversations.md): the facet's reading (canvas plus chat, five-day deployment, 24 participants, "Adoption was uneven", chat stayed central) matches the text. I add that the status is a working draft marked not for distribution.
- [`arteaga2022smart`](../library/arteaga2022smart.md): the facet's quotations and numbers match. One caveat the facet gets right and I confirm: the 58% applies to compliers (the 21.6% who add schools), not to everyone who received the pop-up; for all warned applicants the risk fall is 3.3 points, 13% of the below-threshold mean (pp. 26–27).
- [`ashlagi2018stable`](../library/ashlagi2018stable.md): the facet quotes the abstract correctly and reads the bearing as "formal and not cognitive". The full text shows the claim is about the existence of a bad preference profile, not about every market, and that the paper's own suggestion for cognitive relief is sequential mechanisms, which it says are not OSP either.
- [`bansal2019updates`](../library/bansal2019updates.md): the facet's quotations are correct but it reads the three high-stakes tasks as "crowd participants" ("simulated high-stakes tasks with crowd participants"). The crowd participants played only the abstract CAJA game; the recidivism, mortality and credit-risk work used classifiers alone, with no people. The facet's "participant numbers not in the abstract" is now answered: 25 workers per condition in the mental-model studies (with the bottom quartile of scorers removed as likely spammers, p. 2433); the group sizes for the update study are not stated.
- [`boelhouwer2019should`](../library/boelhouwer2019should.md): facet H says the "mental models did not change." The authors write that the mental models "did not seem to (sufficiently) change" (abstract), inferred from decision accuracy and comments; they did not elicit the models. The facet's "28 participants, null" stands. I add that group 2 was nominally higher and that the information group learned less over the session.
- [`bolton2013engineering`](../library/bolton2013engineering.md): the facet describes the 2013 article as abstract only. This reading is of the 2009 discussion paper, not of the article, so its numbers should not be quoted as the article's.
- [`cabrera2023improving`](../library/cabrera2023improving.md): facet H's second pass says 225 were recruited and 209 analysed. The text removes 13 for failing an attention check and 3 for under 10% accuracy (136:7), which gives 209. The degrees of freedom of the three omnibus tests imply 67, 70 and 68 analysed (205 in all). The paper does not reconcile the two. Facet H's p = 0.048 for birds is confirmed.
- [`cerrone2024school`](../library/cerrone2024school.md): the facet's one-line quotation of the abstract is accurate; the full text adds the Enforced result, which runs the other way (lower truthfulness).
- [`chen2024chatgpt`](../library/chen2024chatgpt.md): facet H had this as abstract only and gave "84% to 51%" and the code-formatting drop. Both hold. The facet's "measures the model, not people" holds. I add that the cleanest evidence is for instruction-following drift, which the authors offer as a partial explanation, not a proven one.
- [`chen2025generative`](../library/chen2025generative.md): facet H lists it as abstract only and says "preference, not performance." That holds. The full text adds the definition of the 72%, the shrinking margin with real users, and the domain split.
- [`crisan2022interactive`](../library/crisan2022interactive.md): facet H says "no performance measure" and "findings are thematic." Agreed. I add the comprehension count for the standard card, and that the authors never test the IMC's effect on understanding the same way.
- [`delacroix2019bottom`](../library/delacroix2019bottom.md): the facet's "legal proposal with no measured effects" is confirmed. The facet lists only title and two authors; the full text shows the interest-conflict argument and the four conditions, which are what make it relevant.
- [`dietvorst2018overcoming`](../library/dietvorst2018overcoming.md): facet H says the abstract was not retrieved and that the claim is "restoring willingness". The full text confirms willingness to use; it adds that willingness was insensitive to the size of the adjustment, and that accuracy fell when adjustment was unrestricted.
- [`ehsan2024seamful`](../library/ehsan2024seamful.md): facet H lists five authors and gives the CSCW citation; the arXiv v2 text confirms five authors. I found no number in the facet to contradict.
- [`fogliato2022who`](../library/fogliato2022who.md): facet H (abstract only) is confirmed on the 19 radiologists, the lower agreement with the AI in the two-step arm "regardless of whether the advice is accurate," and no extra time. The full text adds that the anchoring effect was small in absolute terms (two to six points) and minimal for critical findings, and that several key tests would miss the 0.05 level (the authors use 0.1).
- [`gauthier2026political`](../library/gauthier2026political.md): facet H (abstract only) says exit does not undo exposure through persistent following effects. Confirmed. The authors flag that the asymmetry may also come from who chose the chronological feed: those users differ in observed ways, and "selection on unobserved factors may contribute to this asymmetry" (p. 420). The following mechanism is described as suggestive evidence, and the effects are concentrated among Republicans and Independents, with Democrats largely unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 4).
- [`gero2024supporting`](../library/gero2024supporting.md): facet H (abstract only) says "controlled study n = 24 plus eight case studies; features for comparing many LLM outputs made hard tasks tractable." The numbers are right. The full text shows that "tractable" rests on self-report and one of two tasks, and that the email task showed no difference.
- [`gonczarowski2023strategyproofness`](../library/gonczarowski2023strategyproofness.md): facet H (line 173) says the authors "show with a lab experiment on two elementary mechanisms 'the promise and challenges of menu descriptions'". The October 2025 revision has no experiment, and that phrase does not occur in it. The experiments are in the companion and, per the authors, in the earlier version, which "conduct[ed] an experiment for a second-price auction and median voting" (p. 23; arXiv 2209.13148v2). The facet's abstract came from a different version than the PDF on file.
- [`goyal2025pilot`](../library/goyal2025pilot.md): facet H (line 132) says "seven participants informed the design; ten compared three nested control surfaces within subjects". That matches v2, and the quotation is in the abstract. The facet says the finding "matches Fok and Weld's verification theory (facet B)". This paper does not cite Fok and Weld (I searched the text and reference list), so that link is the facet's and not the authors'.
- [`guess2023how`](../library/guess2023how.md): facet H quotes the abstract and the sample sizes accurately, and calls the study "dyadic" and "the person drops the ranker". The second phrase misdescribes assignment: users were randomised into the chronological feed, not given a choice.
- [`harper2015putting`](../library/harper2015putting.md): facet H records 381 assigned, 168 used the tuner and 148 surveyed, and the 8% self-selection; my reading agrees. It also notes the heavy-user skew (median 186 logins); confirmed in §5.2.
- [`hohenstein2023artificial`](../library/hohenstein2023artificial.md): facet H says "a mediator that writes for one of them" and "a mediator that edits one party's message". The tool offers tap-to-send suggestions the user chooses; it does not write or edit unprompted. The facet's "closer and more cooperative" is the abstract's wording and holds for the partner-use IV result only. The abstract does not say that Google's replies did not raise sentiment against no replies (Study 2), which the body does.
- [`hua2026passive`](../library/hua2026passive.md): facet H quotes the premise as "a friendly, helpful frontier model may disclose its principal's private information unprompted and concede at the first sign of resistance". The abstract reads "a friendly and helpful frontier model may disclose its principal's private information unprompted, and concede the principal's position at the first sign of resistance". The facet quote is a paraphrase and should not be marked as verbatim. The facet's "benchmark" label is loose; the paper trains models as well as evaluating them.
- [`jakesch2019ai`](../library/jakesch2019ai.md): the facet's quotation of the abstract is right. The full text adds that Study 1, with uniform AI labelling, found no effect, which the abstract's "only when" implies but does not report in numbers.
- [`jakesch2023co`](../library/jakesch2023co.md): facet H reads "Abstract only: N = 1,506; an opinionated writing assistant shifted what users wrote and thought." The full text agrees.
- [`kelley2009nutrition`](../library/kelley2009nutrition.md): facet H records this entry as metadata only and rests the 764-participant result on the 2010 CHI paper (`kelley2010standardizing`), which I did not read. This paper has N = 24, not 764.
- [`kling2012comparison`](../library/kling2012comparison.md): n = 406 and 28% against 17% confirmed. The facet's gloss ("computed comparison") omits the default and deadline that the authors list.
- [`li2017obviously`](../library/li2017obviously.md): the facet's "Li 2017 reports a lab experiment" and the 36% / 7% figure are right. My reading puts the figure in §5.3 rather than §5.2, and the 7% compares only the two serial-dictatorship games; the auction pairs use a different measure.
- [`li2026platform`](../library/li2026platform.md): facet H says the guarantee and transparency are bundled, so the reading effect cannot be separated, and it rests on the abstract. The full text is more assertive than that. The authors claim "separate effects" (abstract), but their split (HH against LH, and low against high variance) is indirect. Their own reading of the HH/LH gap, that transparency may matter more than the guarantee, is called only one possible interpretation (p. 22). The facet's caution holds. The 47 million rides figure is the authors' count; the data table counts 1,887,050 driver-weeks.
- [`liu2026sovereignnegotiation`](../library/liu2026sovereignnegotiation.md): facet H quotes "high privacy/consent risk" from an abstract. That phrase is not in the v2 abstract I read, which instead gives faithful success of 6% to 75%, and 48% of agreements breaching a duty. The facet's description ("preprint, benchmark, no human subjects") holds.
- [`lukoff2021how`](../library/lukoff2021how.md): facet H summarises the abstract accurately. Its "(i)-style restructuring, not an added control" reading is only partly borne out. The "high-control" mockups did remove recommendations (restructuring). But the authors' own proposals are mostly controls the user operates: customisation, explicit preferences, a toggle between Explore and Focus modes (§5.3). Users also wanted less control for "ritualized" use. The paper is therefore evidence for context-dependence, not for restructuring over tuning.
- [`lyons2021conceptualising`](../library/lyons2021conceptualising.md): facet H describes this as conceptual and says the dossier card holds the robo-debt quotation. The robo-debt passage is on p. 16 (§6.2). Nothing else in the facet's description needs correction.
- [`matsuo2026educational`](../library/matsuo2026educational.md): facet H lists "n not in abstract". The full text gives N = 45 (15 per group) and the collision counts above. The facet's reading "trigger cues and reasons improved comprehension of limits and cut collisions" overstates the cue: the cue alone gave a small, non-significant timing change and 6 against 7 collisions. The reason carried the result.
- [`mejia2021when`](../library/mejia2021when.md): the facet cites "3,200 requested rides" and the authors; both confirmed. This preprint reports the pre-publication figures; I did not compare them with the journal version.
- [`mitchell2019model`](../library/mitchell2019model.md): facet H lists this paper as "metadata only" and as "a proposal, not a measured effect", type (ii). The full text confirms both. Nothing in it contradicts the facet.
- [`moller2025impact`](../library/moller2025impact.md): facet H quotes the abstract, including "negative spill-over effect on conversations". The main text ties it to the lower-rated replies (Fig. 2d, Table 1) and to the inference that quality falls "even among users not using the AI themselves" (p. 13). I found no separate test of spill-over in the main text, and the supplement is unread, so treat the spill-over as the authors' inference from the reply ratings, not as a separately estimated effect.
- [`nosko2015limits`](../library/nosko2015limits.md): facet H summarises the abstract and calls this type (i), "the mediator doing the work, with no new reading for the buyer". The full text confirms it and adds the authors' own argument for not displaying the measure. The facet marks the source "abstract only"; it can now be cited from the text.
- [`poursabzi2021manipulating`](../library/poursabzi2021manipulating.md): facet H cites only the abstract and says the model-internals result is "evidence about when predictability does not come from transparency". The text supports that. It also shows the mistake-detection result is conditional: it holds in Exps. 1, 2 and 4 (without the message) and not in Exp. 3, which the abstract does not say. A citation of the abstract's sentence without the condition would overstate it.
- [`reesjones2018experimental`](../library/reesjones2018experimental.md): the facet (H, entry for reesjones2018experimental) read this arXiv text in part and its quotations and the AME 0.10 for the NRMP website agree with the full text. No contradiction found.
- [`seira2017are`](../library/seira2017are.md): facet H quotes the abstract accurately. It does not mention that the MTP message raised delinquency, which cuts against a "disclosure is merely inert" reading.
- [`starke2024contesting`](../library/starke2024contesting.md): the facet says "preregistered survey, 6,217 respondents in six countries; 'Approximately 20% of users would opt out...' Intentions only." All correct. One caveat from the full text: the 20% figure counts "I don't know" (24.7%) in the denominator; excluding them the share is 25.7%. The facet's fragment is accurate to the abstract.
- [`suh2023sensecape`](../library/suh2023sensecape.md): the facet quotes the abstract ("explore more topics and structure their knowledge hierarchically") and calls the study "within-subjects", "dyadic" and "abstract only". The full text confirms the quotation and the design and adds that N = 12 and that exploration counts, not decision quality, were the outcome; it also adds the learning-curve costs and the mixed preference result.
- [`terrucha2025humans`](../library/terrucha2025humans.md): the facet says "abstract only," quotes the abstract accurately, and adds "people who delegate contribute more to the public good ... However, they are not more successful." The full text adds a boundary the abstract omits: the contribution gain holds only in the three-level condition, and the success penalty only in the five-level condition (p. 4). This matters if the paper cites the result as a general one.
- [`ueno2026viscanvas`](../library/ueno2026viscanvas.md): the facet says "20 participants, cognitive load and usability 'indistinguishable from current prevailing methods'; more diverse data interaction." The quotation is the abstract's and is accurate. The full text adds that "more diverse" rests on topology counts coded by the authors, not on a count of charts or variables, which were equal, and that only one of eight feature ratings was significant.
- [`wang2024lower`](../library/wang2024lower.md): the facet says "243 users, randomised algorithmic versus chronological timelines, crossover; behaviour changed, perceptions of the platform barely." This matches. The full text adds a point the facet's phrasing could hide: the abstract says "slightly more reliable" news in the algorithmic timeline, but the results report no significant difference in reliability (p. 10), so the headline "higher quality" rests on lower congruence and extremity only.
- [`wang2025evaluating`](../library/wang2025evaluating.md): the facet says "n = 20 business users, self-reported trust and task performance." Two corrections from the full text. First, the abstract states that "Quantitative and qualitative findings indicate that Node-tree interfaces not only improve task performance and decision-making support but also promote higher levels of user trust"; the body gives only percentage descriptives, one non-significant test, and an admission that significance is not reported. Second, "task performance" is a helpfulness rating, not a measured outcome. The facet's reading is therefore too generous if "task performance" is read literally.
- [`zhu2026choose`](../library/zhu2026choose.md): facet H reports the abstract's claim of a significant Delegate gain without the correction. The group effect is p = .033 raw and p = .100 adjusted; the paper itself labels the Delegate results "suggestive". The facet's other numbers (Table 2 counts, Table 3 gaps, 21.6%) match the text.
## Facet I — Understanding through action

- [`brehmer2004achieving`](../library/brehmer2004achieving.md): the facet file's three quotations match the text. The sentence "while the time constants can be seen to happen, dead time and delayed reports require inferences" is the authors' possible explanation of earlier results (Introduction), not a finding of these two experiments.
- [`cen2024measuring`](../library/cen2024measuring.md): facet I read the two-page abstract and reported "1.9 more"; the full paper says "1.9x" and the body counts above. Its bearing line holds.
- [`chernikova2020simulation`](../library/chernikova2020simulation.md): facet I took its bearing from the abstract. The scaffolding-by-prior-knowledge claim is weaker in the body, as shown above. The facet's pairing with Lavoie et al. (transfer) is not made here: Chernikova does not cite Lavoie or Norman, Dore & Grierson, and its outcome tests do not separate transfer to practice.
- [`choi2023creator`](../library/choi2023creator.md): the facet entry (read in part: abstract and 5.2.1) matches. The full text adds that the work-against turn is also driven by values, not only failed blessings (8.1), which the facet does not mention.
- [`cook2021gender`](../library/cook2021gender.md): the facet entry's figure (14% for more than 2,500 against fewer than 100 trips) matches the working paper. The facet entry read the introduction and the returns-to-experience section; the full text adds that the hours-earnings relation turns from convex to concave once experience is measured by trips (Introduction, Section 4), which is a measurement point and not about learning from an algorithm.
- [`dismukes2010checklists`](../library/dismukes2010checklists.md): the facet entry (read in part: p. 4, 6, 23–24) matches. The full text adds the trapping figures (5.6%, 14.4%, 35.4%), which are the report's strongest evidence on monitoring, and its statement that trapping of deviations "appears not to be operating at the level generally assumed" (Section 1.4 and Section 7).
- [`faa2013operational`](../library/faa2013operational.md): the facet entry reads the Executive Summary and findings 1–2; those match. Findings 4 and 10, which this card adds, are the ones that speak to monitoring and over-reliance.
- [`hase2020evaluating`](../library/hase2020evaluating.md): the facet's reading from the abstract holds. One addition: the Prototype tool, which shows the nearest known case, helped in counterfactual tests, so "what-if" displays are not uniformly useless; the Decision Boundary path, closest to a what-if, showed no gain in either test (Tables 1–2).
- [`heiland2023social`](../library/heiland2023social.md): facet I's bearing line, "trial and experience produced theories, some false, and false theories shaped behaviour", is right. It omits the author's own A/B trials, which show deliberate contrast as the exception that worked.
- [`kahneman2009conditions`](../library/kahneman2009conditions.md): the facet quotations (pp. 515, 520, 523, 524) match the text. The facet file marks the read as partial; the full text adds the fractionation argument and the algorithm section above, neither of which the facet entry uses.
- [`kuhl2023alien`](../library/kuhl2023alien.md): the facet's reading from the abstract is right. Added: the knowledge result does not replicate in Experiment 2, and the authors' account that interactivity explains a result that Lim et al. (2009) did not find is untested; they did not compare interactive with passive versions of the same task (p. 14).
- [`mumaw2020analysis`](../library/mumaw2020analysis.md): the facet file read this report only in part. The full text confirms the facet's use for monitoring as a large part of the task. It adds that the authors reject eye-movement training and vigilance training, which the facet does not mention.
- [`rahmandad2023delays`](../library/rahmandad2023delays.md): facet I says "delay and noise push people towards quick-return options and back to their priors". The body separates them. Delay produces the quick-return bias; noise does not (p > 0.9), and it moves people toward the middle. The pull toward priors is strengthened by delay and noise only in study 1 (p. 17), and in study 2 the anchoring did not vary by condition.
- [`smith1995situation`](../library/smith1995situation.md): the facet (I) cites the "Knowledge directs the agent's activity" sentence at pp. 141–142; it falls on p. 141. The abstract quotation is correct (p. 137). The facet's bearing ("acting samples the environment, so 'act or read' is a false pair") matches the text. The text does not say that pilots stop monitoring; it says nothing for or against the pilots-do-not-read claim.
- [`warren2024categorical`](../library/warren2024categorical.md): the facet quotes the published abstract (three studies, N = 127, 136, 211) and says counterfactuals gave higher accuracy than controls but no more than causal explanations, with higher satisfaction and trust. The preprint's Study 1 agrees on each point. The facet's "bearing" line says counterfactual feedback "improves prediction"; the preprint puts the effect at d = .22 and the counterfactual–causal difference at p = .245, so the improvement is small and rests on one pairwise contrast.
- [`weick1988enacted`](../library/weick1988enacted.md): the facet entry (I) calls the article "argued from cases (Bhopal, Mann Gulch)." The article has no Mann Gulch material; its only case is Bhopal. The facet also gives pp. 307–308 for "cognition lies in the path of the action"; the sentence is on p. 307. The facet's other quotations match the text, and its page for "balance dangerous action with safe inaction" (pp. 315–316) is p. 315 in this reading.
## Facet J — Who holds the convention

- [`apple2026guidelines`](../library/apple2026guidelines.md): facet J's quotations and its "no notice period for changes" hold as far as I can see, including the 5.6 restoration clause. Add the regional exceptions and the delegation of duties in 1.2 and 4.7, which facet J did not use.
- [`caperton2009massey`](../library/caperton2009massey.md): the J-facet marked this "read in part (one sentence)" and quoted *Caperton* on recusal from the syllabus-level passage. The opinion supports that use; nothing in the full text contradicts the facet. The facet's point about *Tumey* is confirmed: *Tumey* is the lead case in Part II.A.
- [`cftc2017fxcm`](../library/cftc2017fxcm.md): the J-facet read only the lead paragraph and quoted it accurately ("concealing its relationship," "$7 million," withdraw from registration). The full release adds the 70% rebate and $77 million figure, which the facet does not use.
- [`colvin2011empirical`](../library/colvin2011empirical.md): the J-facet had only the abstract and its summary agrees with the abstract. The full text adds the repeat-player numbers (the abstract only says "significantly lower") and the caveat that the arbitration–litigation comparison is not matched. Nothing in the abstract is contradicted.
- [`douek2023meta`](../library/douek2023meta.md): facet J listed this as metadata only; its "critical reading of the Board" holds. The bib dates it 2023 (the SSRN posting); the journal print is 2024.
- [`eu2019p2b`](../library/eu2019p2b.md): the J-facet read the UK-retained version on legislation.gov.uk and noted that Art. 5(6)–(7) were omitted there. The official EU text contains both: 5(6) is the no-algorithm-disclosure clause above. Facet statements about Arts. 3, 4, 11 and 12 should be rechecked against the pinpoints above (e.g. 15 days' notice, 30 days' notice before termination), since the UK text varied in jurisdictional references.
- [`eu2022dsa`](../library/eu2022dsa.md): I found no quotation in facet J or audit AUDIT_05 that the text contradicts: Art. 14(2), 17(2), 19, 20(6), 21(2) and the dates are as the audit corrected them. Two omissions matter. First, J's list of platform "holders" leaves out Arts. 53 and 54 (complaint to a regulator, damages) and the 6% fine ceiling (Arts. 52(3), 74), which are the Regulation's main enforcement. Second, J:271 ("bound by more written duties ... than an FX dealer") needs the correction in the FX card: Code Principle 40 asks that substantial changes in terms be agreed before trading, while DSA Art. 14(2) asks only that recipients be informed.
- [`evans2018forex`](../library/evans2018forex.md): facet J marked this metadata only. (1) The appendix lists the Financial Stability Board among the authorities "investigating the forex trading activities" of banks; the FSB's report says its work "was completely independent of the various conduct investigations" (`fsb2014foreign`, p. 1). (2) Evans finds extraordinary pre-Fix volatility; the FSB, with seven currencies and April–September 2013, finds the rise in average volatility at the Fix "not especially large" (`fsb2014foreign`, p. 18). The measures differ (tail frequency against mean), so they do not strictly conflict.
- [`fca2014fines`](../library/fca2014fines.md): the J-facet's two quotations ("ineffective controls . . ." and the "attest" language) match the release. The facet's reading is partial but not wrong.
- [`fsb2014foreign`](../library/fsb2014foreign.md): facet J says the change "was proposed by a body of regulators and market participants". Appendix 2 (pp. 33–34) lists only central banks, regulators, the ECB, IOSCO and the FSB secretariat; market participants were consulted (p. 1). Facet J's corrected line, that the report does not say dealers broke a convention, agrees with the text ("allegedly", p. 2).
- [`fsb2015progress`](../library/fsb2015progress.md): the J-facet quoted the 15 February 2015 sentence accurately and read only §2.1. The rest of the report adds the charging and separation findings, the algorithmic shift, and the report's own caution that causes are unclear (p. 13); none of it contradicts the facet.
- [`galanter1974why`](../library/galanter1974why.md): the facet maps the platform to the extreme RP and the driver or seller to a one-shotter. Galanter's own note 4 (p. 97) says welfare clients and taxpayers "are not pure OSs, since there is next year's tax bill and next month's welfare check", and pp. 129–133 predict private ordering where relationships are dense and enduring. A driver is in a continuing, unequal relationship, so the mapping needs that qualification. The facet's p. 111 quotation (arbitration "detached from official sanctions") describes RP-against-RP relations of comparable size, not the platform case.
- [`globalfxc2024code`](../library/globalfxc2024code.md): (1) J:234 and the audit say the Code requires no notice of change to clients. Principle 40 (p. 42) asks that substantial changes to terms be "agreed before any transaction", and Principle 8 (p. 12) asks that a changed capacity be "agreed by both parties". Both are voluntary, but both are stronger than DSA Art. 14(2), which only requires that recipients be informed. (2) The facet's table cell "Hearing/complaint: None in the Code" overlooks Principle 7 (external parties may raise concerns, p. 11) and Principle 39 (client requests for transaction data, p. 42). (3) "Reasons: None required per trade" is right in the narrow sense, but the audit's correction (Principles 9 and 36) also omits that Principle 36 says information "should be made available to Clients upon request" and Principle 39. (4) The edition is December 2024, as the audit found; the bib key and year are still 2021.
- [`jhaver2019suspect`](../library/jhaver2019suspect.md): facet J quoted the abstract only. The abstract's "read community guidelines" clause is not what Table 5 shows, and its 37% rests on 849 coded answers, not 907 respondents.
